report_title: Gaza Cybergang / Molerats (G0021) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK G0021 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0021/) and attributed malware families Spark S0543, DropBook S0547, SharpStage S0546, MoleNet S0553; Palo Alto Unit 42 'Molerats Delivers Spark Backdoor' (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/molerats-delivers-spark-backdoor/); Cybereason 'New Malware Arsenal Abusing Cloud Services in Middle East Espionage Campaign' Dec 2020 (https://www.cybereason.com/blog/new-malware-arsenal-abusing-cloud-services-in-middle-east-espionage-campaign); Cybereason 'Operation Bearded Barbie' Apr 2022 (https://www.cybereason.com/blog/operation-bearded-barbie-apt-c-23-campaign-targeting-israeli-officials); Proofpoint 'NimbleMamba' Feb 2022 (https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/nimblemamba-investigating-ta402-molerats-espionage-trojan); Proofpoint 'TA402 IronWind' Nov 2023 (https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta402-uses-complex-ironwind-infection-chain-target-middle-east); Kaspersky 'Gaza Cybergang Group1 Operation SneakyPastes' Apr 2019 (https://securelist.com/gaza-cybergang-group1-operation-sneakypastes/90068/); MENA-Threat-Actor-Tracker seed (gaza-seed.json)

actor.name: Gaza Cybergang / Molerats
actor.attribution: Palestinian-nexus, Arabic-speaking, politically-motivated espionage group active since at least 2012, per MITRE ATT&CK G0021 and multiple vendor reports (Palo Alto Unit 42, Cybereason, Proofpoint, Kaspersky). Assessed to conduct intelligence collection aligned with Palestinian interests. Note: research clusters within the broader 'Gaza Cybergang' umbrella (Molerats/TA402 vs. APT-C-23/Arid Viper) are tracked variously by vendors; MITRE consolidates the Molerats cluster under G0021. Attribution to a specific sponsoring entity is not publicly established, so nexus (not sponsor) is asserted.

key_campaigns.name: Operation SneakyPastes
key_campaigns.summary: Multi-stage spearphishing campaign using politically-themed lures and paste/file-hosting sites (Pastebin, Github, MyPastebin) as dead-drop stagers to deliver a RAT toolset; targeted Palestinian and broader Middle East political entities and embassies.

key_campaigns.name: Spark backdoor campaign
key_campaigns.summary: Spearphishing with weaponized documents (Israel/Palestine and regional-politics lures) delivering the Spark Windows backdoor; language/geofence checks to ensure Arabic-language victims before execution.

key_campaigns.name: Cloud-services espionage arsenal (SharpStage / DropBook / MoleNet)
key_campaigns.summary: Espionage campaign against high-ranking political and government figures across the Middle East using a new .NET/Python arsenal (SharpStage, DropBook, MoleNet) that abused Dropbox, Google Drive, Facebook, Simplenote and Quora for C2 and exfiltration, blending malicious traffic with legitimate SaaS.

key_campaigns.name: NimbleMamba campaign (TA402)
key_campaigns.summary: Geofenced phishing delivering the NimbleMamba intelligence-gathering implant via RAR archives and actor-controlled domains; C2 and exfiltration over the Dropbox API to blend with normal cloud traffic.

key_campaigns.name: Operation Bearded Barbie (Pierogi)
key_campaigns.summary: Social-engineering campaign using elaborate fake social-media personas to lure Israeli individuals into installing the Pierogi backdoor and mobile malware for espionage, screen capture and file theft. Attributed by Cybereason to the APT-C-23/Gaza Cybergang cluster.

key_campaigns.name: IronWind infection-chain campaign (TA402)
key_campaigns.summary: Multi-stage IronWind loader delivered through Middle East government-themed lures, using varied initial-access vectors (Dropbox links, XLL Excel add-ins, and Microsoft Access .accdb files) and HTML smuggling to stage shellcode downloaders for follow-on espionage tooling.

ttps.procedure_description: Gaza Cybergang sends spearphishing emails with malicious Microsoft Word/Excel and PDF attachments carrying regional-politics lures (Israeli-Palestinian affairs, Hamas/Fatah, diplomatic themes) to deliver Spark, SharpStage and IronWind.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — attachment-based spearphishing is detectable via mail sandboxing and macro/XLL/.accdb content analysis at the gateway

ttps.procedure_description: Gaza Cybergang sends phishing emails containing malicious links, including geofenced links (NimbleMamba) and Dropbox-hosted links (IronWind) that gate delivery to intended regional victims.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link-based spearphishing is detectable via URL rewriting/detonation and proxy telemetry, though geofencing degrades sandbox coverage

ttps.procedure_description: Sends malicious links via email that trick users into opening a RAR/archive and running an embedded executable.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link clicks are visible in email/URL-gateway and proxy logs; endpoint signal is indirect until the archive is opened

ttps.procedure_description: Delivers files via email that trick users into clicking Enable Content to run an embedded macro, or into opening weaponized XLL/.accdb files leading to IronWind.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Office/Excel spawning script or child processes after macro/XLL enablement is a core detectable behavior

ttps.procedure_description: Uses PowerShell implants and PowerShell execution stages (observed in SharpStage and MoleNet chains).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — script-block/module logging and suspicious PowerShell parenting (Office->PowerShell) are well-covered detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Spark, SharpStage, DropBook, MoleNet and Pierogi execute commands via the Windows command shell (cmd.exe).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe execution with anomalous parents (Office, script hosts, backdoor processes) is visible in process-creation logs

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttps.procedure_description: Uses various implants built with VBScript on target machines, including macro-embedded VBS droppers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — wscript/cscript executing VBS, especially spawned by Office, is a strong detectable signal

ttps.procedure_description: DropBook is a Python-based backdoor compiled with PyInstaller, executing Python-implemented backdoor logic on the victim.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — PyInstaller-packed binaries are detectable via unusual temp _MEI extraction folders and bundled-python process behavior rather than a python.exe command line

ttps.procedure_description: Uses various implants including those built with JavaScript on target machines.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — wscript/mshta-hosted JS is detectable via script-host process lineage and script-block logging

ttps.procedure_description: SharpStage and MoleNet use WMI for execution and host reconnaissance.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — WMI process creation and WMI-Activity operational logs provide strong telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Creates scheduled tasks to persistently run VBScripts and to relaunch the SharpStage backdoor.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation is logged (Event ID 4698 / Task Scheduler operational) and highly detectable, especially with script actions

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: Saves malicious files within AppData and Startup folders and sets Run keys to maintain persistence (SharpStage, MoleNet).
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Run-key writes and Startup-folder file drops are detectable via registry and file-creation telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: The IronWind multi-stage loader downloads and injects shellcode into a target process to run follow-on stages in memory.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — injection is detectable via EDR memory/API telemetry (CreateRemoteThread, RWX allocations) but requires endpoint depth

ttps.procedure_description: Uses msiexec.exe to execute an MSI payload as a proxy for malicious code execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — msiexec.exe executing MSI packages from user-writable/temp paths or with network sources is a detectable LOLBin pattern

ttps.procedure_description: Uses forged/abused Microsoft code-signing certificates on malware to appear trusted.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — signed-malware is detectable via certificate-reputation/thumbprint hunting and signature-anomaly analytics on loaded binaries

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
ttps.procedure_description: The Spark backdoor is packed (Enigma protector) to hinder static analysis and detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — packed binaries are common and packing alone is weakly indicative; hunt candidate via packer-signature/entropy analytics rather than a standalone alert

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling
ttps.procedure_description: IronWind initial-access chains use HTML smuggling to reconstruct and drop the malicious archive/payload client-side, evading gateway inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTML smuggling is detectable via JS blob/anchor-download inspection at the proxy and browser-download telemetry, but bypasses attachment scanning

ttps.procedure_description: Delivers compressed executables within ZIP/RAR files to victims to evade content inspection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — archive delivery is ubiquitous; better as gateway archive-inspection/hunt than a standalone endpoint detection

ttps.procedure_description: Decompresses ZIP files once on the victim machine and decodes staged/encoded payloads at runtime (Spark, SharpStage, DropBook).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — runtime decode routines are detectable via script-block logging and certutil/PowerShell decode command-lines where used

ttps.technique_name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: User Activity Based Checks
ttps.procedure_description: Spark performs anti-analysis/user-activity checks before executing to avoid detonating in sandboxes.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — pre-payload sandbox/user-activity checks leave little host log signal; hunt candidate via static analysis of the sample

ttps.technique_name: System Location Discovery: System Language Discovery
ttps.procedure_description: Spark, DropBook and SharpStage check the system's keyboard/language settings so the malware runs only on Arabic-language systems; NimbleMamba similarly geofences delivery — a signature Gaza Cybergang victim-gating behavior.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — a single locale/keyboard-layout API query is near-invisible in host logs; hunt candidate via sample analysis, not endpoint detection

ttps.procedure_description: Spark, DropBook, SharpStage and MoleNet collect host information (OS, hostname, hardware) and report it to C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — systeminfo-style discovery is common; suspicious mainly in tight backdoor process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: Spark gathers the victim's username/owner information as part of host profiling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami/user-context queries are common; value is in process-lineage correlation with the backdoor

ttps.procedure_description: DropBook enumerates files and directories on the victim to select data of interest.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — file/directory enumeration is high-volume and hard to isolate; behavioral hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: MoleNet enumerates installed security/AV software on the victim to inform follow-on tooling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — AV-product enumeration (WMI SecurityCenter / registry / service queries) is detectable when tied to a backdoor's process lineage

ttps.procedure_description: Obtains a list of active processes on the victim and sends them to C2 servers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — process enumeration is common but meaningful in backdoor process-lineage context

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttps.procedure_description: Uses the public tool BrowserPasswordDump10 to dump passwords saved in victim browsers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — access to browser Login Data stores and known-tool execution are detectable via file-access and process signatures

ttps.procedure_description: SharpStage and the Pierogi backdoor capture screenshots of the victim's desktop for espionage.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — screen-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Uses executables and backdoors (DropBook, SharpStage, MoleNet, IronWind, Pierogi) to download additional malicious files and follow-on stages onto the victim.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — remote downloads and unexpected inbound file writes are strongly detectable in process + network telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Spark and IronWind communicate with C2 over HTTP/web protocols.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP C2 is detectable via proxy/beacon analytics and URI/JA3 anomalies but blends with normal web traffic

ttps.procedure_description: Spark encodes C2 data using standard encoding (e.g. base64) before transmission.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — base64-encoded C2 content is detectable via network inspection and encoding heuristics where TLS is absent

ttps.procedure_description: DropBook and SharpStage use legitimate web/cloud services (Dropbox, Google Drive, Facebook, Simplenote, Quora) as the C2 medium to blend with normal SaaS traffic — a signature Gaza Cybergang tradecraft.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — cloud-service C2 rides trusted SaaS domains and TLS; not detectable by domain reputation alone. Hunt candidate via anomalous process-to-SaaS-API behavior (backdoor/PyInstaller process talking to Dropbox/Facebook APIs) and CASB/egress analytics

ttps.procedure_description: DropBook receives commands and NimbleMamba tasks/returns data through the Dropbox/Facebook/Simplenote APIs, using the cloud service for full bidirectional C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — bidirectional SaaS-API C2 is indistinguishable from legitimate cloud use at the network layer; hunt candidate via endpoint process-behavior baselining and cloud-app API-token anomaly detection

ttps.procedure_description: Spark exfiltrates collected victim data back over its established C2 channel.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — exfil over the C2 channel is detectable via outbound-volume/beacon analytics on the same session, but blends with C2 traffic

ttps.procedure_description: DropBook exfiltrates stolen data to attacker-controlled cloud-service accounts rather than dedicated C2 infrastructure.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — exfil to trusted SaaS blends with sanctioned cloud use; hunt candidate via DLP/CASB upload-volume anomalies and unusual process-to-cloud API activity

ttps.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
ttps.procedure_description: NimbleMamba and DropBook exfiltrate collected files to actor-controlled Dropbox cloud storage.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — uploads to Dropbox are trusted by default; hunt candidate via CASB/egress upload-size anomalies and non-browser processes calling cloud-storage APIs

detection_signals: Office application (winword/excel) or an XLL add-in / Microsoft Access (msaccess.exe) spawning wscript.exe/powershell.exe/cmd.exe shortly after document open (SharpStage / IronWind delivery)
PyInstaller runtime artifacts — _MEIxxxxx extraction folders in %TEMP% and a bundled-python process making outbound Dropbox/Facebook API calls (DropBook)
Non-browser / backdoor process communicating with api.dropboxapi.com, content.dropboxapi.com, graph.facebook.com, simplenote or Google Drive APIs (cloud-service C2 — DropBook/SharpStage/NimbleMamba)
Anomalous outbound upload volume to Dropbox / cloud storage from an endpoint with no user-driven browser session (T1567.002 exfil)
Scheduled task creation (Event ID 4698) or Run-key/Startup-folder writes launching payloads from AppData (SharpStage/MoleNet persistence)
msiexec.exe executing an MSI from a user-writable/temp path or remote source
HTML file that reconstructs and triggers a download client-side (JS blob + anchor download) — HTML smuggling (IronWind)
BrowserPasswordDump10 execution or access to browser Login Data stores by a non-browser process
wscript/cscript executing VBS or JS spawned by an Office parent (SneakyPastes / macro droppers)
Process performing a keyboard-layout/locale check immediately followed by exit on non-Arabic systems (language-gating — visible mainly in sample/sandbox analysis, not host logs)
notes: TTP set built primarily from MITRE ATT&CK G0021 (16 group-level techniques) and enriched to 36 techniques using the technique mappings MITRE attributes to this actor's malware families — Spark (S0543), DropBook (S0547), SharpStage (S0546), MoleNet (S0553) — plus well-sourced public reporting for families MITRE does not yet map under G0021 (NimbleMamba/Proofpoint Feb 2022, IronWind/Proofpoint Nov 2023, Pierogi/Cybereason Apr 2022). 20 techniques were added beyond the 16-technique seed: T1027.002, T1027.006, T1033, T1041, T1047, T1055, T1059.003, T1059.006, T1071.001, T1082, T1083, T1102, T1102.002, T1113, T1132.001, T1497.002, T1518.001, T1567, T1567.002, T1614.001 (T1053.005 was already in the seed, additionally corroborated here via SharpStage). Every added technique carries a source citation to the MITRE software page and/or the originating vendor report. Attribution asserted as Palestinian-NEXUS (not a named sponsor) at high confidence per MITRE G0021 and four independent vendors; note the 'Gaza Cybergang' umbrella spans clusters (Molerats/TA402 = G0021 here; APT-C-23/Arid Viper tracked separately by some vendors) and the Pierogi/Bearded Barbie campaign is attributed to the APT-C-23 sub-cluster by Cybereason — retained under this pack per the tracker seed but flagged. SIGNATURE TRADECRAFT and its honest feasibility: cloud-service C2 and cloud exfiltration (Dropbox/Google Drive/Facebook/Simplenote) are the defining Gaza Cybergang behavior and are all LOW detection-feasibility — they ride trusted SaaS over TLS and cannot be caught by domain reputation; they are hunt candidates (endpoint process-to-SaaS-API baselining, CASB/DLP upload-anomaly analytics), not signature detection candidates. LOW detection-feasibility techniques (route to hunting, not detection): T1102 (Web Service C2), T1102.002 (Bidirectional Web Service C2), T1567 (Exfil Over Web Service), T1567.002 (Exfil to Cloud Storage), T1614.001 (language-gating), T1497.002 (sandbox checks), T1027.002 (software packing), T1027.015 (archive compression), T1083 (file/dir discovery), T1113 (screen capture). IOCs are deliberately EMPTY: concrete host-independent indicators (C2 SaaS account handles, staging domains, sample hashes) are enumerated in the named Unit 42 / Cybereason / Proofpoint / Kaspersky reports and should be ingested directly from those sources before being asserted here — none are reproduced from memory to avoid fabrication. No CVE is characteristic of this actor (initial access is social-engineering-driven), so cves is empty.
